stem: A 34-year-old woman has had a dry cough and progressive dyspnea on exertion for 3 months. Chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary function tests show a reduced FEV1 and diffusing capacity. Transbronchial biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas. Stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungi are negative.
oneliner: 34F + 3 mo cough, dyspnea + bilateral hilar adenopathy + reduced FEV1 and DLCO + noncaseating granulomas + AFB and fungal stains negative → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate initial treatment?

whyNot.A: **Steroid-sparing** agent used if prednisone fails or is not tolerated
whyNot.C: **Steroid-sparing** agent used if prednisone fails or is not tolerated
whyNot.D: For **tuberculosis**; stains are negative and the granulomas are noncaseating
whyNot.E: **TNF inhibitor** reserved for disease that fails steroids and steroid-sparing drugs

why: **Bilateral hilar adenopathy + noncaseating granulomas + symptoms** = symptomatic sarcoidosis. **Glucocorticoids** are first line and suppress the **granulomatous T-cell and macrophage response**.

drug.name: Prednisone
drug.how: Binds the cytosolic receptor and alters gene transcription: less cytokine production and T-cell activity
drug.use: Sarcoidosis, autoimmune disease, asthma, transplant, adrenal insufficiency
drug.watch: Cushingoid features, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, cataracts, infection risk, adrenal suppression

stem: A 48-year-old woman has had 5 weeks of painful, swollen small joints of both hands with 2 hours of morning stiffness. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are positive. Methotrexate is started, but she can barely grip a pen and asks for something that will help her function while the methotrexate takes effect over the next 2 to 3 months.
oneliner: 48F + 5 wk symmetric hand arthritis + 2 h morning stiffness + RF and anti-CCP positive + methotrexate just started + needs short-term relief → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to add for short-term relief?

whyNot.A: **TNF inhibitor** reserved for patients who **fail** methotrexate, not a bridge
whyNot.B: **TNF inhibitor** reserved for patients who **fail** methotrexate, not a bridge
whyNot.C: **Slow-acting gold** that takes months, like the drug she just started
whyNot.D: **Slow-acting DMARD** that takes months to work

why: **New RA on a slow DMARD** needs a **bridge**. Low-dose **prednisone** relieves inflammation within days while the DMARD takes weeks to months.

drug.name: Prednisone
drug.how: Binds the cytosolic receptor and alters gene transcription: less cytokine production and T-cell activity
drug.use: Bridge therapy in RA, autoimmune disease, asthma, transplant, adrenal insufficiency
drug.watch: Cushingoid features, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, cataracts, infection risk, adrenal suppression

stem: A 45-year-old man has had well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on his elbows, knees, trunk and scalp for 6 years, now covering about 30% of his body surface, with nail pitting. Coal tar, calcipotriene and triamcinolone cream have not controlled it. He drinks no alcohol, has normal liver tests and kidney function, and is not planning children.
oneliner: 45M + 6 y plaque psoriasis on 30% of body + nail pitting + failed coal tar, calcipotriene, triamcinolone + normal liver and kidneys, no alcohol → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to add?

whyNot.B: Too toxic and **not used** for psoriasis
whyNot.D: An **antibiotic** for acne and rosacea; no effect on psoriasis
whyNot.E: A **topical retinoid** for acne and photoaging; not a systemic psoriasis drug

why: **Extensive plaque psoriasis refractory to topical therapy** needs a **systemic agent**; **methotrexate** blocks dihydrofolate reductase and slows hyperproliferating keratinocytes and immune cells.

drug.name: Methotrexate
drug.how: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking thymidine and purine synthesis
drug.use: Psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, ALL, lymphoma, ectopic pregnancy
drug.watch: Myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis, teratogenic; leucovorin rescue

stem: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has had persistent swollen joints and morning stiffness for 4 hours despite 6 months of weekly methotrexate and low-dose prednisone. Chest x-ray and a tuberculosis screening test are negative, and hepatitis B serology is negative. Her rheumatologist plans to add a drug that blocks a pro-inflammatory cytokine.
oneliner: 52F + RA + persistent synovitis despite 6 mo methotrexate and prednisone + negative TB and hepatitis B screens + next drug blocks a cytokine → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?

whyNot.A: Activates **macrophages** (used in chronic granulomatous disease); would **worsen** inflammation
whyNot.B: **Interleukin-2** expands T cells; used in melanoma and renal cell carcinoma
whyNot.C: **GM-CSF**, a growth factor that raises neutrophils; not an RA therapy
whyNot.D: **IL-11**, raises platelets; not an RA therapy

why: **RA inadequately controlled on methotrexate** is escalated to a **TNF-alpha inhibitor** such as **adalimumab**, after screening for latent TB and hepatitis B.

drug.name: Adalimumab
drug.use: Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, Crohn disease
drug.watch: Reactivation of latent TB, serious infections, demyelination, lymphoma

stem: A 7-year-old boy with chronic granulomatous disease has an absent oxidative burst on dihydrorhodamine testing and has had repeated staphylococcal abscesses. His physician wants long-term prophylaxis in addition to antibiotics and an antifungal.
oneliner: 7M + chronic granulomatous disease + absent DHR burst + recurrent Staph abscesses + long-term prophylaxis → which recombinant cytokine?
ask: Which recombinant cytokine is added for prophylaxis?

whyNot.A: Antiviral and antitumor use (**hepatitis B**, hairy cell leukemia); does not restore phagocyte killing
whyNot.B: Used for **multiple sclerosis**; no effect on his missing burst
whyNot.C: Expands T and NK cells for **renal cell carcinoma and melanoma**; not a phagocyte activator
whyNot.E: Raises neutrophil **numbers**; his neutrophils are present but **cannot make the burst**

why: CGD neutrophils are normal in number but lack **NADPH oxidase**, so catalase-positive organisms survive. **Interferon-gamma** enhances phagocyte killing and cuts serious infections; it is given with **TMP-SMX and itraconazole** prophylaxis.

idea.rule: Match the cytokine to its disease: IFN-gamma for CGD, IFN-alpha for hepatitis, IFN-beta for MS.
also: IL-2 for renal cell carcinoma and melanoma
Erythropoietin for anemia of renal disease

drug.name: Interferon-gamma
drug.how: Activates macrophages and improves their killing of ingested microbes
drug.use: Chronic granulomatous disease (infection prevention), with TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis
